You must select the deployment type (Multi-AZ or Single-AZ), storage type (SSD or HDD), storage capacity (32 to 65,536 GiB for SSD; 2,000 to 65,536 GiB for HDD), and throughput capacity (8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, or 2048 MB/s). Throughput capacity is the attribute that contributes most to the overall attainable performance and throughput of a file system. However, there are three resource components that significantly impact a file system\u2019s overall throughput: network throughput, in-memory cache, and disk throughput. These components are illustrated in the following diagram (*Figure 1*).\\\\n\\\\n*Figure 1 \u2013 performance components of an Amazon FSx for Windows File Server*\\\\n\\\\nThe performance section of the Amazon FSx user guide has a comprehensive table that shows the disk, in-memory cache, IOPS, and network throughput for all possible throughput capacities. {"id": "4af4e7c6-c552-44bb-8df7-da8985667abe", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Low throughput on an FSx for Windows File Server is almost always tied to the **throughput capacity setting** you provisioned — this single attribute determines three resource ceilings, and hitting any one of them will bottleneck performance:

1. **Network I/O** – the speed the file server can serve data to clients. Lower throughput capacity tiers cap this (e.g., at 8 MB/s throughput capacity, baseline network is just 8 MB/s; it scales up to 1500 MB/s baseline at 1024 MB/s capacity).
2. **File server CPU and memory** – also governs in-memory caching. Less cache means more requests fall through to disk, which is slower. Low throughput tiers get very little cache (e.g., 0.5 GB at the 8 MB/s tier vs. 64 GB at 1024 MB/s).
3. **Disk I/O** – the speed between the file server and backing storage volumes, which also scales with throughput capacity.

**Common root causes of low throughput:**

- **Undersized throughput capacity** — the file system is provisioned below what the workload needs. AWS explicitly notes that throughput capacity levels below 32 MB/s are meant for test/dev, not production.
- **Cache exhaustion** — working set exceeds the memory allocated for caching at your tier, forcing more disk reads.
- **Disk throughput saturation** — especially relevant on HDD storage type, which has much lower disk throughput than SSD.
- **Network throughput ceiling reached** — many small/concurrent client connections can hit the network cap before disk or CPU become the bottleneck.
- **Storage type choice** — HDD storage has significantly lower baseline/burst disk throughput than SSD; workloads needing high IOPS or throughput on HDD will bottleneck quickly.
- **Region-specific limits** — the highest throughput tiers (4,608 MB/s and above) are only available in a subset of regions (us-east-1, us-west-2, us-east-2, eu-west-1, ap-northeast-1, ap-southeast-1).

The fix in most cases is scaling up the throughput capacity (and/or switching storage type from HDD to SSD), since that single setting governs network, cache, and disk ceilings together.

Want me to pull up the actual throughput capacity, storage type, and current utilization metrics for one of your FSx for Windows file systems to see which of these is the bottleneck?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
